 Recovery Of Victim's Ornaments Alone Cannot Prove Murder: Supreme Court Acquits Man
 Saima Anjum 
 19 Nov 2026 4:41 PM IST
 Share this 
 Listen to this Article The Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 18) set aside the conviction of a man for the murder of a woman, observing that the prosecution had failed to establish a complete and unbroken chain of circumstantial evidence as the recovery of victim's ornaments alone cannot prove murder.
 A bench of Justice Prashant Kumar Mishra and Justice Vipul M Pancholi observed so while hearing an appeal filed against the Karnataka High Court's judgment which had upheld appellant's (accused) conviction under Section 302 Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC, now Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023/BNS) and the sentence of life imprisonment imposed by the Sessions Court. 
 The deceased woman's body was found stuffed inside an iron drum in Harapanahalli in 2013. It is alleged that the appellant was in an illicit relationship with her and suspected her of being involved with another man. Out of rage, the accused strangled her with a plastic strap and robbed her of her ornaments. It was also alleged that the accused led the police to his house from where gold and silver ornaments were recovered. 
 The Sessions Court rejected the 'last seen together' evidence of two witnesses (PW 13 and PW 14) because of an unexplained delay (58 days) in recording their statements. Instead, it sustained the conviction on the basis of the recovery of the ornaments. However, it acquitted the appellant for causing disappearance of evidence under Section 201 IPC (now Section 238 of the BNS). The High Court, however, considered the 'last seen together' evidence, confirming the conviction and sentence. 
 Aggrieved by the High Court's finding, the accused approached the Supreme Court.
 Before the Supreme Court Senior Advocate A Sirajudeen argued for the appellant that the case rested wholly on circumstantial evidence and that the principles in Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v State of Maharashtra were not satisfied. It was contended that motive was unproved and that the discovery of the body was improbable. It was also submitted that the High Court had relied on the 'last seen' evidence of the witnesses without addressing the Session Court's finding on the 58-day delay. Relying on Sanwat Khan v State of Rajasthan and Raj Kumar @ Raju v State (NCT of Delhi) , it was argued that recovery of the ornaments could not sustain a murder conviction.
 On the contrary, Additional Advocate General Avishkar Singhvi argued for the respondent (prosecution) that motive and homicidal death were proved, that the appellant had given no explanation for the recovery of the ornaments and that the theft and the homicide formed a single transaction.
 Perusing the submissions, the Supreme Court noted that motive is of vital importance in a case resting on circumstantial evidence. It held that both Session Court and the High Court erred “by treating the general knowledge of an illicit relationship as proof of the motive to commit murder.” The bench noted that the deceased's nephew (PW 5) and husband (PW 7) admitted that they had no personal knowledge of the alleged relationship. It also noted that none of the witnesses said the appellant suspected the deceased of involvement with another man, or that any quarrel had taken place with regards to it.
 “PW-5 admitted during cross-examination that he did not personally witness any illicit relationship between the deceased and the appellant and further admitted that he had informed the police that he merely suspected the appellant in connection with the deceased's death. Similarly, PW-7 admitted that he had no personal knowledge of the affair. Significantly, none of the prosecution witnesses testified that the appellant harboured suspicion that the deceased was involved with another man or that any quarrel had ever taken place between them on that account. Thus, we are of the opinion that the motive alleged by the prosecution is a matter of conjecture and surmise, which cannot be accepted as an established circumstance against the appellant.” 
 Referring to Kanhaiya Lal v State of Rajasthan , the bench reiterated that the circumstance of 'last seen together' does not by itself lead to an inference of guilt, unless there is proximate and independent corroborative material linking the accused to the crime. 
 With regards to the Session Court's rejection of statements of PW 13 and PW 14 recorded under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC, now Section 180 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023/BNSS), the bench observed as under: 
 “The Trial Court rightly took note of this unexplained delay and expressly rejected their testimonies, holding that “the evidence is not believable to rely on the last seen theory”. However, the High Court relied upon their testimonies without addressing the 58-day delay or providing any reasoning for reversing the said finding of the Trial Court. Thus, we are of the view that where the delay in recording the statements remains completely unexplained, the “last seen” evidence is not conclusively established and was rightly rejected by the Trial Court.” 
 The Court further noted that the prosecution's story of the discovery of the body had inconsistencies as the informant who allegedly informed the complainant (PW 1) about the body was neither traced nor examined, and neither the inquest report nor the post-mortem report showed any trace or stain of limestone on the deceased's clothing or person. On this, the bench observed that it creates doubt as to the veracity of the prosecution version regarding the discovery of the body.
 The bench found the recovery doubtful as one of the three panch witnesses to the seizure was not examined. PW 23 did not mention his presence, and neither PW 12 nor PW 23 testified to the disclosure statement made by the appellant. In the absence of independent evidence supporting the disclosure, the Court held that the essential prerequisites under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (now Section 23 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023/BSA) remain unsatisfied. It also noted that PW 12 admitted that the contents of the seizure were dictated by the investigating officer and that he did not know the house from which the trunk was retrieved. The bench also took note that PW 23, the appraiser, admitted that he was a regular police witness, that his signature was struck out without explanation. 
 The bench also noted that the prosecution failed to prove that the deceased was actually wearing the recovered ornaments when last seen alive with the appellant. However, PW 13 and PW 14 did not mention any jewellery. PW 8 (son) had left a day earlier, while PW 10 and PW 11 did not depose to seeing her leave with the appellant. It was also observed that considering the alleged relationship, it was natural and plausible that some of her belongings might have been kept at his house. PW 13 admitted that the day after the incident, the police told him the deceased's earrings and gold effects had already been found at the appellant's residence, which contradicted the prosecution's timeline of recovery. 
 The Court noted that the only motive advanced was personal animosity arising out of the relationship, and that no motive for theft of the jewellery was established. Further note was taken of the fact that no charge under Sections 379, 392, or 404 IPC (now Section 303(2), 309(4), or 315 of the BNS) was framed against the appellant.
 Relying on Sanwat Khan as reaffirmed in Raj Kumar @ Raju , the bench reiterated that unexplained possession of articles belonging to the deceased only enables a presumption under Illustration (a) to Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act (now Section 119 of the BSA) regarding theft or receipt of stolen property. 
 “Therefore, in the present case, in the absence of cogent evidence showing that the robbery/theft and murder formed part of the same transaction, we are of the view that such recovery, by itself, cannot be stretched to infer guilt of the appellant for murder under Section 302 IPC,” the bench observed. 
 The bench also reiterated the observation in Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade v State of Maharashtra as “Certainly, it is a primary principle that the accused must be and not merely may be guilty before a court can convict and the mental distance between 'may be' and 'must be' is long and divides vague conjectures from sure conclusions.” 
 Applying the above, the Supreme Court held that the chain of circumstantial evidence cannot be said to be complete and that the findings of guilt were based on conjectures and surmises. The appellant's conviction and sentence was, therefore, quashed, given the benefit of doubt. 
 “On a holistic consideration of the evidence on record, the chain of circumstantial evidence cannot be said to be complete and unbroken. The prosecution has failed to establish the circumstances pointing conclusively to the guilt of the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. The findings of guilt recorded by the Trial Court and confirmed by the High Court are based on conjectures and surmises. Therefore, the appellant is entitled to the benefit of doubt and the conviction under Section 302 IPC cannot be sustained in law.” 
 “The conviction of the appellant under Section 302 IPC as well as the sentence of imprisonment for life and fine imposed by the Trial Court in Sessions Case No. 101 of 2014 and affirmed by the High Court of Karnataka in the final judgment and order dated 09.07.2024 in Criminal Appeal No. 1355 of 2017, are hereby quashed and set aside, however, the acquittal of the appellant under Section 201 IPC by the Trial Court is maintained. Consequently, the appellant is acquitted for the offence punishable under Section 302 IPC.” 
 Appearances:
 For Appellant: Mr. A. Sirajudeen, Sr. Adv.; Ms. Jyotika Kalra, AOR; Mr. Inderdeep Singh, Adv.; Ms. Sonakshi Shankar Dikshit, Adv.
